lessons.title: Jobs
lessons.scenario: Smarty welcomes Mia and Sam to his workshop and shows pictures of common jobs.

items.example: My grandfather is a farmer.
items.note: Say 'farmer' for a person who grows food and keeps animals like cows and sheep.

image.describe: an orange cat wearing a straw hat and blue overalls standing by a red barn with a friendly cow

items.example: The pilot is in the plane.
items.note: Use 'pilot' when you talk about the person who flies a plane.

image.describe: a gray cat in a dark blue pilot uniform and cap sitting in the cockpit of a small plane

items.example: Her uncle is a driver.
items.note: Say 'driver' for a person who drives a car, bus, or train.

image.describe: a brown cat wearing a cap and holding the steering wheel of a yellow bus

items.example: Sam is a good mechanic.
items.note: Use 'mechanic' for a person who fixes cars and motorbikes.

image.describe: a black-and-white cat in blue overalls holding a metal tool beside an open car hood

items.example: The builder is wearing a yellow hat.
items.note: Say 'builder' for a person who builds houses, schools, and walls.

image.describe: a ginger cat wearing a yellow hard hat and tool belt standing beside a brick wall

items.example: I visited the dentist yesterday.
items.note: Use 'dentist' when you talk about a doctor who takes care of your teeth.

image.describe: a white cat in a clean white coat smiling next to a dentist chair and small mirror

grammar.title: a or an with jobs
grammar.explanation: Put a or an before a singular job word. Use a before a consonant sound (a farmer, a pilot) and an before a vowel sound (an actor).

practice.prompt: Who has cows and sheep and works on the land?
practice.explanation: A farmer works with animals like cows and sheep.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The pilot is in the plane.
practice.answer: The pilot is in the plane.
options: The pilot is in the plane.
The driver is in the car.
The builder is in the room.
practice.explanation: A pilot flies a plane.

practice.prompt: Match each job with the place or thing.
practice.explanation: A pilot flies a plane, a driver drives a car, a farmer keeps cows, and a teacher works at a school.

practice.prompt: My tooth hurts! Who should I visit?
practice.explanation: A dentist helps you when your tooth hurts.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about Sam.
practice.explanation: Put 'a' before 'good mechanic'.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about the person in a yellow hard hat.
practice.text: The ___ is wearing a yellow hat.
practice.explanation: A builder wears a yellow hard hat at work.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about a hospital worker.
practice.text: My aunt is a ___ at the hospital.
practice.explanation: A doctor works at a hospital.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: Her uncle is a driver.
practice.explanation: Remember to say 'a' before 'driver'.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you about the jobs of people in your family. Any real or imaginary answer is great.

turns.smarty: My uncle is a pilot. Is your father a farmer or a driver?
turns.hint: Say 'My father is a…' and name a job.

turns.smarty: Cool! And what about your mother or aunt? Is she a dentist or a builder?
turns.hint: Say 'She is a…' and choose a job.

turns.smarty: Who helps when a car stops? A mechanic or a pilot?
turns.hint: Name the person who fixes cars.

lessons.title: More jobs
lessons.scenario: Leo and Zara visit Smarty's workshop and learn six more job names.

items.example: The police officer helped my brother.
items.note: Say 'police officer' for a person who keeps people safe in town.

image.describe: a gray tabby cat in a neat blue police uniform and peaked cap standing near a crosswalk

items.example: A firefighter is strong and fast.
items.note: Use 'firefighter' for a person whose job is to stop fires.

image.describe: an orange cat wearing a yellow firefighter coat and helmet holding a water hose beside a red fire truck

items.example: Mia is an engineer.
items.note: Say 'engineer' for a person who designs machines, bridges, or computers.

image.describe: a black-and-white cat wearing safety glasses looking at machine plans on a desk

items.example: An artist loves to draw and paint.
items.note: Use 'artist' for a person who paints, draws, or makes art.

image.describe: a calico cat wearing a beret and holding a paintbrush in front of a colorful canvas

items.example: The chef cooked delicious soup.
items.note: Say 'chef' for a person who cooks food in a restaurant or hotel.

image.describe: a white cat wearing a tall white chef hat and apron stirring a pot in a kitchen

items.example: The nurse is at the hospital.
items.note: Use 'nurse' for a person who cares for ill people in a hospital.

image.describe: a cream-colored cat wearing blue medical scrubs and holding a clipboard in a bright hospital room

grammar.title: Using an before vowel sounds
grammar.explanation: Words like engineer and artist start with a vowel sound, so put an before them instead of a.

practice.prompt: Who cooks delicious food in a restaurant?
practice.explanation: A chef cooks food in a restaurant.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The nurse is at the hospital.
practice.answer: The nurse is at the hospital.
options: The nurse is at the hospital.
The chef is at the restaurant.
The artist is at the museum.
practice.explanation: A nurse helps ill people at the hospital.

practice.explanation: An artist draws and paints, a chef cooks, a mechanic works on cars, and a pilot flies a plane.

practice.explanation: A firefighter stops fires.

practice.prompt: Choose the right word before 'engineer'.
practice.text: Mia is ___ engineer.
practice.explanation: 'Engineer' starts with a vowel sound, so use 'an'.

practice.explanation: Say 'chef' with a 'sh' sound at the start.

lessons.title: What do you do?
lessons.scenario: Ben and Ana meet Smarty in the workshop and talk about their jobs and hours.

items.example: Hello, Ben! What do you do?
items.note: Ask 'What do you do?' when you want to know someone's job.

items.example: I work as a mechanic.
items.note: Say 'I work as a…' right before the name of your job.

items.example: I work for a big hospital.
items.note: Use 'I work for…' before the place or group that pays you.

items.example: She has a full-time job at the bank.
items.note: Say 'a full-time job' when you work every day, usually five days a week.

items.example: I have a part-time job at a café.
items.note: Use 'a part-time job' when you work only a few hours or days each week.

items.example: Pilot is my dream job.
items.note: Say 'my dream job' for the job you wish for most of all.

grammar.title: I work as vs. I work for
grammar.explanation: Use 'I work as' before your job title (I work as a nurse). Use 'I work for' before the place or organization (I work for a hospital).
examples: I work for a big restaurant.

practice.prompt: You meet a new friend and want to ask about their job. What do you say?
practice.explanation: 'What do you do?' is the natural way to ask about someone's job.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.explanation: Use 'I work as' before a job name like 'mechanic'.

practice.prompt: Match the sentence halves.
practice.explanation: 'Work as' goes with a job; 'work for' goes with a workplace.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence with the right phrase.
practice.text: ___ a chef at a hotel.
practice.explanation: 'A chef' is a job title, so use 'I work as'.

practice.prompt: Ana works at a school. Complete her sentence.
practice.text: ___ a small school in town.
practice.explanation: 'A small school' is the place she works, so use 'I work for'.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about a Monday-to-Friday job.
practice.explanation: A job all week is 'a full-time job'.

practice.prompt: Ben is a student and works only on Saturday and Sunday. What does he have?
practice.explanation: Working only on the weekend is 'a part-time job'.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: Pilot is my dream job.
practice.explanation: Use 'my dream job' for the job you love most.

story.hook: Does Ben have a full-time job or a part-time job?

questions.explanation: Ana says: I work as an engineer.

lessons.title: Rules at work
lessons.scenario: Smarty puts on a safety helmet in the workshop and explains work rules to Tom and Mia.

items.example: I have to wear a helmet at work.
items.note: Say 'I have to…' when a rule or job says you need to do something.

items.example: I do not have to work on Sunday.
items.note: Use 'I do not have to…' when something is not needed and you can choose.

items.example: A firefighter must be fast.
items.note: Say 'must' for an important rule that everyone needs to follow.

items.example: You must not run in the room.
items.note: Use 'must not' to say a rule forbids something—never do it!

items.example: Builders must wear a helmet.
items.note: Say 'wear a helmet' for putting a hard hat on to protect your head.

items.example: We must be on time for work.
items.note: Use 'be on time' when you arrive at the right hour and are not late.

grammar.title: must, must not, and do not have to
grammar.explanation: Use 'must' or 'have to' for rules. Use 'must not' when something is forbidden. Use 'do not have to' when something is not required.
examples: I do not have to work on Sunday.

practice.prompt: What must a builder put on their head at work?
practice.explanation: Builders must wear a helmet to keep their head safe.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: You must not run in the room.
practice.answer: You must not run in the room.
options: You must not run in the room.
I do not have to run.
practice.explanation: 'Must not' means running is forbidden.

practice.prompt: Match each rule phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: 'Must not' forbids something, while 'do not have to' means it is not needed.

practice.prompt: Sunday is a free day! Choose the right phrase.
practice.text: ___ work on Sunday.
practice.explanation: You can rest on Sunday, so 'I do not have to' is right.

practice.prompt: This rule says: NEVER use your phone in class. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Students ___ look at a phone in the lesson.
practice.explanation: When something is forbidden, use 'must not'.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about a rule at work.
practice.answer: I have to wear a helmet.
practice.explanation: Use 'I have to' + 'wear a helmet'.

practice.prompt: Work starts at nine o'clock. Complete the rule.
practice.text: A pilot must ___.
practice.explanation: A pilot cannot be late—they must be on time.

practice.prompt: Mia is a chef. She wears a white hat, not a hard hat. Which sentence is true?
practice.answer: She does not have to wear a helmet.
options: She does not have to wear a helmet.
She must not be on time.
practice.explanation: A chef does not need a helmet, so 'does not have to' is true.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: We must be on time for work.
practice.answer: We must be on time for work.
practice.explanation: Say 'must be on time' smoothly.

story.hook: What rule does Smarty give Tom and Mia in the work room?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat wearing a yellow safety helmet in his workshop, handing a second helmet to Tom while Mia checks a wall clock.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Good morning, Tom and Mia! Look at the clock—you are on time.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Yes! We know we must be on time.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Here is rule two: you must wear a helmet in this room.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Okay! I have to wear a helmet. What about shoes?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: You must wear boots, and you must not run here.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Do we have to work on Sunday?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: No! You do not have to come on the weekend.

questions.prompt: What must Tom and Mia wear in the room?
questions.explanation: Smarty says: you must wear a helmet, and you must wear boots.

questions.prompt: What must Tom and Mia NOT do?
questions.explanation: Smarty says: you must not run here.

questions.prompt: Do Tom and Mia have to work on Sunday?
questions.answer: No, they do not have to.
options: No, they do not have to.
questions.explanation: Smarty says: You do not have to come on the weekend.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you about rules at your school or job.

turns.smarty: At work, we must be on time. Do you have to be on time at school or work?
accept: ^yes(?: i have to be on time| i must be on time| i do)?$
turns.example: Yes, I have to be on time.
turns.hint: Say 'Yes, I have to be on time.'

turns.smarty: Tell me one thing you must not do at school or work.
turns.hint: Say 'I must not…' (for example: run, sleep, or be late).

turns.smarty: What about Sunday? Do you have to work or study on Sunday?
accept: ^no(?: i do not have to(?: work| study)?(?: on sunday)?)?$
^i do not have to (?:work|study)(?: on sunday)?$
turns.example: No, I do not have to work on Sunday.
turns.hint: Say 'No, I do not have to work on Sunday.'

lessons.title: Tools
lessons.scenario: Smarty opens his big red toolbox in the workshop and shows Sam six useful tools.

items.example: Please give me the hammer.
items.note: Say 'hammer' for the heavy tool you swing to hit nails.

image.describe: a metal claw hammer with a smooth wooden handle lying on a wooden workbench

items.example: This small screwdriver is on the table.
items.note: Use 'screwdriver' for the hand tool that turns screws.

items.example: A mechanic always has a wrench.
items.note: Say 'wrench' for the metal tool that holds and turns nuts and bolts.

items.example: The hammer is in the toolbox.

lessons.title: Dreams
lessons.scenario: Smarty, Lily, and Leo sit in the workshop and talk about their dreams for the future.

items.example: I want to be an engineer.
items.note: Say 'I want to be a…' to tell someone what job or person you wish to become.

items.example: I would like to be a pilot.
items.note: Use 'I would like to be…' as a polite, warm way to talk about your future dream.

items.example: One day, I want to visit Brazil.
items.note: Say 'one day' when you mean at some time in the future.

items.example: My dream is to help animals.
items.note: Start with 'My dream is to…' when you share your biggest wish or goal.

items.example: When I grow up, I want to be a chef.
items.note: Kids say 'When I grow up…' to talk about what they will do as an adult.

items.example: I hope to work as a nurse.
items.note: Use 'I hope to…' for something good you wish will happen in the future.

grammar.title: I want to be vs. I would like to be
grammar.explanation: Both 'I want to be' and 'I would like to be' talk about your dreams. 'I would like to be' sounds a little softer and more polite.
examples: I want to be an artist.
I would like to be a doctor one day.

practice.prompt: How do you say your future job wish?
practice.answer: I want to be a pilot.
options: I want to be a pilot.
I must not be a pilot.
practice.explanation: Use 'I want to be' for a job you wish to have.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: I would like to be an engineer.
practice.answer: I would like to be an engineer.
options: I would like to be an engineer.
I want to be a chef.
practice.explanation: 'I would like to be' is a polite way to share your dream.

practice.prompt: Match the sentence beginnings and endings.

pairs.right: I want to be a chef.

practice.explanation: Notice how 'My dream is' and 'I hope to' are followed by a verb.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about the future.

practice.explanation: 'When I grow up' talks about the future when you are an adult.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about your biggest dream.
practice.answer: My dream is to visit England.
practice.explanation: Use 'My dream is to' + verb.

practice.prompt: Complete Leo's sentence.
practice.text: ___ work as a nurse one day.
practice.explanation: 'Work' is a verb, so 'I hope to work' fits here.

practice.prompt: Add the phrase that means 'in the future'.
practice.text: I would like to be a chef ___.
practice.explanation: 'One day' means at some time in the future.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: I want to be an engineer.
practice.answer: I want to be an engineer.
practice.explanation: Say 'want to be' clearly.
